chunks: "I'd draw frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical.
For a periodic signal the spectrum is discrete lines, spaced at the repetition frequency f0, which is one over the period.
There's a line at DC equal to the average, then lines at f0, 2f0, 3f0 and so on. The line heights follow a sinc envelope that depends on the pulse width tau.
The nth harmonic has amplitude 2 volts times the absolute value of sine of n pi D, over n pi, where D is the duty cycle.
The envelope first goes to zero at 1 over tau, so the nulls fall at multiples of f0 over D.
For a 50% square wave that means the first null is at the second harmonic, so only odd lines survive, and they go as 1 over n: 1, one third, one fifth.
For a 25% pulse train every fourth harmonic is missing. A narrower pulse spreads the energy out: the envelope is wider, so more harmonics have similar height.
If I'm being careful, I'd add that a real pulse has a finite rise time, which multiplies the envelope by a second sinc.
Above a knee near 1 over pi times the rise time, the lines fall at 40 decibels per decade instead of 20.
A single non-repeating pulse has the same envelope, but as a continuous curve, not lines."
